missions/american-board-mission/name: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM)
missions/american-board-mission/statusNo: In 1961, following the formation of the United Church of Christ, the ABCFM was merged into the United Church Board for World Ministries; since 1995–96 its work has continued in the Common Global Ministries Board of the UCC and the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ). Most of its fields had long since become autonomous churches, colleges and hospitals.
missions/american-board-mission/summary: The first major American foreign missionary society, born of the Second Great Awakening and the 1806 Haystack Prayer Meeting at Williams College. Largely Congregationalist (with Presbyterian and Dutch Reformed partners until the 1830s–1870), it sent missionaries to India, Ceylon, Hawaii, the Cherokee and other Native nations, the Ottoman Empire, China, Japan, southern Africa and Micronesia, and through its long-serving secretary Rufus Anderson became, with Henry Venn's CMS, the chief theorist of the 'three-self' indigenous church.
missions/american-board-mission/story:
The American Board grew out of a student movement. In August 1806 a group of Williams College students led by Samuel J. Mills Jr sheltered from a thunderstorm beside a haystack and prayed for the 'heathen' world; the 'Haystack Prayer Meeting' became a founding legend of American missions. Several of the group went on to Andover Theological Seminary, where in June 1810 Adoniram Judson, Samuel Nott, Samuel Newell and Samuel Mills petitioned the General Association of Massachusetts. The Association created the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions on 29 June 1810 at Bradford, Massachusetts. Its theology was the 'New Divinity' Calvinism of Samuel Hopkins and the heirs of Jonathan Edwards: an urgent concern for the salvation of souls joined to a postmillennial confidence that the spread of the gospel, schools and Christian civilisation would usher in the kingdom of God.

On 6 February 1812 five men were ordained at the Tabernacle Church in Salem and within days sailed for India with their wives, among them Ann Hasseltine Judson and Harriet Newell. The East India Company, still hostile to missionaries, ordered them away; the Judsons and Luther Rice became Baptists on the voyage and left the Board (giving rise to the American Baptist mission in Burma), Harriet Newell died in Mauritius, and only Gordon Hall and Samuel Nott eventually established a mission at Bombay in 1813. Further missions followed in northern Ceylon (Jaffna, 1816, with the Batticotta seminary from 1823), Ahmednagar (1831) and Madura (1834) — fields that produced some of the most educated Tamil and Marathi Protestant communities in Asia.

At home and in the Pacific the Board pursued a 'civilising' as well as an evangelistic programme. Among the Cherokee (Brainerd, 1817) and Choctaw (1818) it ran schools and churches; when Georgia imprisoned the missionaries Samuel Worcester and Elizur Butler for refusing to obey its laws on Cherokee land, the case produced the Supreme Court's Worcester v. Georgia (1832), which upheld Cherokee sovereignty but was not enforced, and missionaries accompanied the Cherokee on the Trail of Tears. In 1819–20 the brig Thaddeus carried Hiram Bingham and Asa Thurston to Hawaii, where the chiefs had just abolished the kapu system. The mission devised a Hawaiian alphabet, printed the Bible (completed 1839), founded schools that made Hawaiians among the most literate peoples of the age, and saw a mass revival in 1837–40, when Titus Coan at Hilo baptised about 1,700 people on a single day in July 1838. In the Oregon Country, by contrast, the mission of Marcus and Narcissa Whitman ended in their killing by Cayuse in 1847 after a measles epidemic.

The Ottoman mission was the Board's most ambitious. Pliny Fisk and Levi Parsons sailed in 1819 hoping to reach Jews and Muslims in Palestine; in practice the Board's converts came overwhelmingly from the ancient Eastern churches, above all Armenians. William Goodell and H. G. O. Dwight in Constantinople, Eli Smith and Cornelius Van Dyck in Beirut (whose Arabic Bible of 1865 is still widely used) and a dense network of schools, colleges (Robert College, 1863; the Syrian Protestant College, 1866, later the American University of Beirut; Anatolia, Euphrates and Central Turkey colleges) and hospitals made American Protestants a significant presence in the empire. When Armenian Protestants were excommunicated by their patriarch, the Ottoman government recognised a separate Protestant community (1847, by firman in 1850). Board missionaries witnessed the Hamidian massacres of 1894–96 and the Armenian genocide of 1915; Board secretary James L. Barton chaired what became Near East Relief.

Rufus Anderson, foreign secretary from 1832 to 1866, gave the Board its classic strategy. Like Henry Venn of the CMS, he argued that the goal of mission was not to reproduce New England but to plant self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating churches under native pastors, after which the missionary should move on. His deputation to India in 1854–55 cut back English-language education in favour of vernacular preaching and native pastorates — a contested decision later partly reversed. Hawaii was declared a Christian land and the Board withdrew its support in 1863 in favour of the Hawaiian Evangelical Association; Presbyterian and Reformed partners left to form their own boards (the Syria mission passed to the Presbyterians in 1870).

The Board also entered China (Elijah Bridgman in Canton, 1830, the first American Protestant missionary there, and Peter Parker's hospital), southern Africa (the Zulu mission from 1835, with Inanda and Adams College), Micronesia (from 1852, using a series of mission ships named Morning Star), Japan (1869, where it backed Niijima Jō in founding Doshisha in Kyoto in 1875) and Angola (1880). In the Boxer rising of 1900 its North China and Shanxi missionaries — many from the Oberlin Band — were killed at Baoding, Taigu and Fenzhou along with Chinese converts; the subsequent indemnity-gathering by Board missionary William Ament became a public scandal attacked by Mark Twain. By the 1920s the Board stood near the liberal end of American Protestantism and supported the Laymen's Inquiry of 1932. It merged into the United Church Board for World Ministries in 1961.
missions/american-board-mission/beliefs/: Edwardsean 'New Divinity' Calvinism: humanity is lost without Christ, and the call to 'disinterested benevolence' obliges Christians to seek the conversion of the whole world.
Postmillennial optimism that the worldwide spread of the gospel, Bible, schools and Christian civilisation would precede and prepare for Christ's millennial reign.
The supreme authority of Scripture and the necessity of its translation into every vernacular so that converts could read it for themselves.
A Congregational ecclesiology in which local churches govern themselves — the theological root of Rufus Anderson's 'three-self' ideal.
Moral reform as part of the gospel: temperance, Sabbath observance, monogamy, the abolition of infanticide and (for many but not all members) of slavery.
In the later 19th and 20th centuries, a gradual move toward liberal theology, the social gospel and an emphasis on service, education and medicine rather than conversion alone.
missions/american-board-mission/strategi: Founding schools, seminaries and colleges (Batticotta, Robert College, Doshisha, Anatolia College, Adams College) to train an educated native ministry and elite.

Reducing unwritten languages to writing (Hawaiian, Cherokee printing with Sequoyah's syllabary, Zulu, Micronesian languages) and printing Bibles and tracts on mission presses at Malta, Beirut, Smyrna and Honolulu.
Rufus Anderson's 'three-self' policy: ordaining native pastors, handing churches self-government and withdrawing missionaries once a church could stand alone.
Targeting the ancient Eastern churches of the Ottoman Empire as a bridge to Muslims — in practice creating Armenian, Greek and Arab Protestant communities.
Medical missions, from Peter Parker's eye hospital in Canton (1835) to hospitals across Anatolia, India and China.
Recruiting large numbers of women, first as missionary wives and from 1868 through the Woman's Board of Missions, as teachers, doctors and evangelists to women.
Mission ships (the Morning Star series) and stations linked by printing and correspondence across the Pacific.
missions/american-board-mission/groupsRe: Native Hawaiians, whose chiefs and commoners largely adopted Protestant Christianity between 1820 and the 1840s.
Cherokee, Choctaw, Dakota and other Native American nations, among whom the Board ran schools and churches before and after Removal.
Armenians, Greeks, Syrian and Lebanese Arabs and Bulgarians of the Ottoman Empire, mainly converts from Eastern Christian churches.
Tamils of Jaffna and Madurai and Marathi-speakers around Ahmednagar, including many from Dalit and lower-caste communities.
Zulu-speaking communities of Natal, especially around Inanda, Amanzimtoti and Umvoti.
Chinese of Canton, Fuzhou, North China and Shanxi; Japanese students and samurai-class converts around Doshisha.
Micronesians of Pohnpei, Kosrae, the Marshall and Gilbert Islands, often through Hawaiian Christian missionaries.
missions/american-board-mission/challeng: Very high mortality and illness among early missionaries and their children, from Harriet Newell's death in 1812 to fevers in Africa and India.
Opposition from the East India Company before 1813 and from the patriarchates and Ottoman authorities, who saw proselytising among Eastern Christians as subversive.
Removal of the Cherokee and other nations by the United States, which destroyed the Board's southern Native missions despite Worcester v. Georgia.
The slavery question: the Board accepted slaveholding Cherokee converts and was slow to condemn slavery, provoking the abolitionist breakaway American Missionary Association (1846).
Massacre and war: the Whitman killings (1847), the Boxer rising (1900), the Hamidian massacres (1894–96) and the Armenian genocide (1915) destroyed whole stations and congregations.
Theological conflict at home, from Old School–New School Presbyterian quarrels to the 'Andover controversy' over future probation (1880s) and later fundamentalist–modernist disputes.
missions/american-board-mission/harms/0: In Hawaii, missionaries suppressed the hula, traditional religion and much of Hawaiian culture, and some missionary families (and their descendants such as Sanford Dole and Lorrin Thurston) became central to the sugar economy and the 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy.
missions/american-board-mission/harms/1: Boarding schools and 'civilisation' programmes among Native Americans promoted assimilation and the suppression of Native languages and practices, even where missionaries defended Native land rights.
missions/american-board-mission/harms/2: The Ottoman mission drew members away from the Armenian, Greek and Syrian churches, causing bitter schism and inviting suspicion of Christian minorities as agents of foreign powers.
missions/american-board-mission/harms/3: After the Boxer rising, Board missionary William Ament's collection of punitive indemnities and confiscated property from Chinese villages caused a scandal and damaged the reputation of missions in China.
missions/american-board-mission/harms/4: Cultural paternalism and assumptions of Anglo-American superiority often delayed the very three-self independence the Board officially championed.
missions/american-board-mission/harms/5: Early tolerance of slaveholding among Native American church members compromised its witness and split its supporters.
missions/american-board-mission/developm: Rufus Anderson's 'three-self' theory, developed alongside Henry Venn's, became the dominant Protestant goal of mission for a century and shaped later indigenous church movements.
Literacy, printing and Bible translation in Hawaiian, Arabic (the Smith–Van Dyck Bible, 1865), Armenian, Bulgarian, Zulu, Tamil and Marathi.

Enduring institutions: Doshisha University, the American University of Beirut (via the Syrian Protestant College), Robert College (Istanbul), Jaffna College, the American College in Madurai and Adams College.
Pioneering women's mission work through the Woman's Board of Missions (1868), which sent hundreds of single women teachers and doctors.
Missionary witness and relief during the Armenian genocide, leading to Near East Relief, one of the first large humanitarian campaigns.
The ecumenical heritage of mission later carried into the United Church of Christ and Disciples' Global Ministries.
missions/american-board-mission/outcome: In its 150 years the ABCFM sent several thousand missionaries and left behind autonomous churches (the Hawaiian Evangelical Association, the Jaffna Diocese of the Church of South India, the Kumiai churches in Japan, the United Congregational Church of Southern Africa, Armenian Evangelical churches), a remarkable network of schools, colleges and hospitals, and the classic statement of the three-self ideal. In 1961 it merged into the United Church Board for World Ministries.

missions/american-board-mission/countrie: India (Bombay, Ahmednagar, Madura)
Gordon Hall and Samuel Nott opened Bombay in 1813; Ahmednagar (1831) and Madura (1834) became strong Marathi and Tamil missions with schools, the American College and hospitals.
Sri Lanka (Jaffna)
A Tamil mission with the Batticotta seminary (1823) and Uduvil girls' school produced one of the best-educated Protestant communities in Asia.
Cherokee Nation and other Native nations (USA)
Brainerd Mission (1817) and Choctaw missions (1818) ran schools and churches; Worcester v. Georgia (1832) and Removal shaped the work.
Hawaii
From 1820 the mission devised a Hawaiian alphabet, translated the Bible and saw mass revival; support was transferred to the Hawaiian Evangelical Association in 1863.
Ottoman Empire (Turkey, Syria/Lebanon)
Missions at Smyrna, Beirut and Constantinople created Armenian and Arab Protestant communities, a large school system and colleges.
China
Elijah Bridgman opened Canton in 1830; later missions in Fuzhou, North China and Shanxi lost many workers in the Boxer rising.
South Africa (Natal)
The Zulu mission founded stations at Inanda, Amanzimtoti and Umvoti and later Adams College.
Micronesia
Missionaries and Hawaiian Christians worked from Pohnpei and Kosrae to the Marshall and Gilbert Islands, served by the Morning Star ships.
Japan
Supported Niijima Jō in founding Doshisha (1875) and the Kumiai (Congregational) churches.
Angola
A mission among the Ovimbundu at Bailundo and Chissamba led to the Evangelical Congregational Church of Angola.
missions/american-board-mission/journeys: The first American missionaries sail for India (1812–13)
Adoniram and Ann Judson, Samuel and Harriet Newell, Samuel Nott, Gordon Hall, Luther Rice

After their ordination at Salem in February 1812 the first Board missionaries sailed for Calcutta. Ordered out by the East India Company, the Newells went to Mauritius, where Harriet died; Hall and Nott reached Bombay in 1813 and founded the Board's first mission, while the Judsons and Rice, now Baptists, left the Board.
Hiram and Sybil Bingham, Asa and Lucy Thurston and the first Sandwich Islands company

The brig Thaddeus left Boston in October 1819 with seven missionary couples and Hawaiian youths educated at the Foreign Mission School in Cornwall, Connecticut, rounded Cape Horn and reached Kailua-Kona in March–April 1820, where King Liholiho allowed them to stay; the Binghams went on to Honolulu.
Fisk and Parsons to the Levant (1819–21)

The Board's 'Palestine Mission' sailed from Boston in November 1819, reached Smyrna via Malta in 1820, and Parsons visited Jerusalem in 1821. Both died young (1822 and 1825), but their reconnaissance launched the Ottoman missions in Beirut and Constantinople.
missions/american-board-mission/relation: Three of the Board's first missionaries — Adoniram and Ann Judson and Luther Rice — adopted believer's baptism on the voyage of 1812, left the Board and became the founders of American Baptist foreign missions in Burma.
Rufus Anderson and Henry Venn corresponded and independently formulated the 'three-self' goal; CMS and Board missions cooperated in South India, Ceylon and the Near East.

The Haystack tradition and the children of Board missionaries (notably Robert Wilder, son of Royal Wilder of the Kolhapur mission) were central to the founding of the Student Volunteer Movement in 1886.

The Board became a leading member of the Foreign Missions Conference, the International Missionary Council and later the WCC orbit before merging into the United Church Board for World Ministries in 1961.
missions/american-board-mission/agreemen: Shared the 'three-self' goal of self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating churches, articulated by Anderson and Venn in the 1840s–50s.
Like the LMS, a Congregational and nominally non-denominational society that combined evangelism with education and 'civilisation', especially in the Pacific.
Shared a commitment to higher education as a means of forming a Christian elite, as in Robert College, Doshisha and the Batticotta seminary.
missions/american-board-mission/disagree: Parted with the Judsons and Rice over infant baptism in 1812, creating separate Congregational and Baptist missionary structures in America.
The Board's denominational-board model of guaranteed salaries, institutional work and (by 1900) liberal theology contrasted with the CIM's faith principle and focus on itinerant evangelism.
By the 1920s the Board's support for the social gospel and the Laymen's Inquiry put it at odds with conservative faith missions that stressed conversion and biblical inerrancy.
missions/american-board-mission/deviatio: Founded to convert the 'heathen' and Muslims, the Ottoman mission in practice won converts mainly from existing Eastern Christian churches.
Although it championed native-led churches, missionaries often retained control of money and institutions for decades.
Rufus Anderson's anti-institutional vernacular policy of the 1850s was abandoned later in the century as the Board invested heavily in colleges and hospitals.
By the 1920s–30s the Board had moved from Edwardsean evangelical Calvinism toward theological liberalism and a service-centred understanding of mission.
